title: Abstract

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: In 2024 the Korea Baseball Organization became the first top-tier league to replace the home-plate umpire’s ball–strike judgment with an automated system. Using over a million pitches from 2021 to 2026, we separate the change into the removal of human discretion and the imposition of a new zone geometry. The machine eliminated count-dependent calls, the value of catcher framing and a small advantage for star batters, rents worth only a few runs per player-season. Because the machine’s zone scales with height and treats every matchup alike, it redistributed strikes toward tall batters and across matchups; but few pitches are exposed to these changes, and their effects on plate-appearance outcomes are precisely estimated and close to zero. Pitchers re-optimized quickly by throwing higher, with left-handers catching up to an existing trend, whereas we find no evidence that batters adjusted. The results suggest that the incidence of replacing human judgment with a rule depends on its geometry and on exposure. Keywords: automated ball-strike system; algorithmic decision-making; evaluator bias; rents; adaptation JEL classification: Z22, J24, D83, O33

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Algorithms increasingly replace human judgment in decisions about people, from hiring and lending to bail and grading. A large literature asks whether such algorithms decide better than the humans they replace ( Kleinberg et al., 2018 ; Hoffman et al., 2018 ) . Less is known about what the replacement does to the people being evaluated. Removing human discretion should eliminate the advantages that discretion created, but a rule also has a shape. The shape determines who gains and who loses, and those affected may or may not change their behavior in response. Answering these questions requires a setting in which every decision is recorded, the rule that replaces human judgment is known, and the behavior of those being evaluated can be observed before and after the change. Professional baseball offers such a setting. Every pitch is tracked, every ball–strike call (the umpire’s ruling on a pitch the batter does not swing at) is recorded, and the call is the outcome of a judgment that, until recently, was made by a human umpire. In 2024 the Korea Baseball Organization (KBO) became the first top-tier professional league to hand that judgment entirely to an automated ball-strike system (ABS). The ABS calls a strike whenever any part of the ball passes through a rectangle defined by each batter’s registered height. We study this change using every regular-season pitch thrown in the KBO from 2021 to 2026, more than a million pitches. We combine the pitches with the tracking system’s trajectories, the umpires assigned to each game, and the catcher on the field for each pitch. We organize the analysis around a simple decomposition. Relative to a human umpire, the machine changes calls in two ways. It removes the discretionary component of human judgment, that is, the part of the call that responds to context such as the count (the number of balls and strikes so far in the plate appearance), the batter’s reputation or the catcher’s receiving skill. It also imposes a new geometry , the difference between the zone the rule defines and the zone humans actually called. The first component is a set of rents created by the evaluator; the second is a redistribution chosen by the rule’s designers. To a first approximation, the economic incidence of either component equals the number of calls it changes per plate appearance (a batter’s turn at bat) times the value of a ball relative to a strike. Finally, those affected should adapt only when the gain from adapting exceeds its cost. Three sets of findings emerge. First, the machine removed the rents created by human discretion. On border pitches, those close to the edge of the zone, human umpires were 6.1 percentage points more likely to call a strike when the batter was ahead in the count (2-0, 3-0 or 3-1) and 6.7 points less likely with two strikes; neither adjustment is detectable under the ABS. Catcher framing, the skill of receiving pitches so that umpires call them strikes, was persistent under human umpires, with split-half reliabilities between 0.60 and 0.81, and it became indistinguishable from noise under the machine. Human umpires also gave star batters slightly fewer called strikes on border pitches, although the size of this effect depends on how finely location is held fixed. Valued at what a strike costs the batting team in expected runs, these rents amounted to a few runs per catcher-season and about one run per star batter-season. Second, the geometry of the rule redistributed strikes along two margins, but the redistribution had little effect on outcomes. Because the human zone was anchored in absolute height while the machine’s zone scales with registered height, the ABS moved strikes toward taller batters at the top of the zone: relative to the human zone, each centimeter of height added 0.75 percentage points to the share of a batter’s high pitches that were called strikes. Because human umpires treated pitcher–batter matchups asymmetrically, the machine also moved strikes between handedness matchups at the edges. Few pitches are exposed to these changes, however. The extra strikes amount to at most one in every 23 plate appearances, and ten centimeters of height change the probability that a plate appearance reaches two strikes or three balls, one call away from a strikeout or a walk, by less than two percentage points. Third, pitchers adapted and batters did not. Using the change in each location’s value under the machine as a measure of treatment intensity, we find that pitchers reallocated their pitches toward locations the ABS favored, quickly and almost entirely through pitch height. The acceleration at the time of the ABS comes from left-handed pitchers. Right-handed and side-arm pitchers (those who throw with a low, sideways arm angle) had already been raising their pitches before 2024, whereas left-handed pitchers had not, and they caught up within a season. For batters, by contrast, we detect no change in swing decisions, either in response to the new geometry or to the end of count-dependent calls. This asymmetry is consistent with a simple cost of re-optimization. A pitcher’s plan is set in advance and applies to every batter, whereas a batter decides in real time, and the stakes for any one batter are small. The paper contributes to four literatures. A body of work in economics and management documents that human evaluators in sport are influenced by race ( Price and Wolfers, 2010 ; Parsons et al., 2011 ; Tainsky et al., 2015 ; Hamrick and Rasp, 2015 ) , status ( Kim and King, 2014 ; Mills, 2014 ) , nationality ( Zitzewitz, 2006 ) , the sequence of past decisions ( Chen et al., 2016 ) , the count ( MacMahon and Starkes, 2008 ) , and the home crowd ( Sutter and Kocher, 2004 ; Garicano et al., 2005 ; Dohmen, 2008 ; Hsu, 2024 ) , and that the quality of their judgment varies with working conditions ( Fesselmeyer, 2021 ) . A related set of studies shows that these biases respond to the evaluator’s environment: favoritism fell when referees became full-time professionals ( Rickman and Witt, 2008 ) and when referees became aware of their bias ( Pope et al., 2018 ) , and pitch-tracking technology changed how umpires called the zone ( Mills, 2017 ; Hunter, 2018 ; Bradbury, 2019 ) . These studies observe human evaluators under different incentives and degrees of scrutiny. We observe the complete replacement of the evaluator, which allows us to measure the rents that discretion created and to test whether they vanish. Our results also relate to the economics of algorithmic decision-making ( Kleinberg et al., 2018 ; Hoffman et al., 2018 ) . That literature compares the quality of human and machine decisions. We show that the distributional consequences of replacing humans with a rule are governed by the rule’s geometry and by exposure, and that those evaluated by the rule may not adapt to it. Third, we add to the evidence on how professional agents adjust their strategies when payoffs change. Some studies find that professionals play close to optimally ( Walker and Wooders, 2001 ; Chiappori et al., 2002 ; Palacios-Huerta, 2003 ; Abramitzky et al., 2012 ) and change their strategies as theory predicts when the rules change ( Banerjee et al., 2007 ) , while others document persistent departures from optimal play ( Romer, 2006 ; Kovash and Levitt, 2009 ) . That pitchers adapted to the ABS while batters did not suggests that which pattern prevails depends on how much an agent stands to gain from re-optimizing. Finally, we build on recent studies of the ABS itself. Lee et al. (2025) describe how the zone changed in the first half of 2024, and Lee and Ko (2026) show that count-dependent calls disappeared, a result we replicate. Song et al. (2026) attribute a decline in star batters’ performance after the ABS to the loss of umpire favoritism. We find evidence of this favoritism at the level of individual calls, but its value appears small, and much of the decline in outcomes appears to reflect the choice of a single pre-ABS season as the baseline. The rest of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 develops the conceptual framework and the hypotheses. Section 3 describes the institutional setting and the data, and Section 4 the empirical strategy. Section 5 presents the results and their robustness, and Section 6 concludes.

sections.heading: 2.1 Setup
sections.text: Consider a pitch that the batter does not swing at, a taken pitch. It crosses the middle plane of home plate at location ℓ \ell (horizontal position and height), is thrown to a batter of registered height h h , and arrives in a context θ \theta . The context comprises the count, the batter’s reputation, the catcher, and the home-plate umpire. The evaluator calls a strike with probability S ⁡ ( ℓ , h , θ ) S(\ell,h,\theta) . Under a human umpire, S H ​ ( ℓ , h , θ ) S^{H}(\ell,h,\theta) is a smooth function of location. It may also depend on the context, through count adjustments, deference to reputation, or the catcher’s receiving skill, and it need not scale with the batter’s height. Under the ABS, the call is the indicator S M ( ℓ , h ) = 𝟏 { ℓ ∈ Z ( h ) } . S^{M}(\ell,h)=\mathbf{1}\{\ell\in Z(h)\}. (1) Here Z ⁡ ( h ) Z(h) is the zone defined by the league’s rules ( Korea Baseball Organization, 2026 ) . Its vertical bounds are fixed fractions of registered height, and its width is the plate (43.18 cm) plus 2 cm on each side; Section 3 gives the details. By construction, ∂ S M / ∂ θ = 0 \partial S^{M}/\partial\theta=0 . The switch from S H S^{H} to S M S^{M} in 2024 is the shock we study. Let v s ​ ( θ ) v_{s}(\theta) and v b ​ ( θ ) v_{b}(\theta) be the batter’s expected plate-appearance value after a called strike and after a called ball in count θ \theta , and let Δ ​ v ​ ( θ ) = v b ​ ( θ ) − v s ​ ( θ ) > 0 \Delta v(\theta)=v_{b}(\theta)-v_{s}(\theta)>0 . We estimate v v from 2022–2023 plate appearances, measuring the value of a plate appearance by weighted on-base average (wOBA), which weights each outcome (walk, single, home run and so on) by its average contribution to run scoring and gives outs a weight of zero. We call the weight of a plate appearance’s final outcome its plate-appearance value ; a player’s wOBA is the average of these values. On average, one strike is worth 0.135 runs.

sections.heading: 2.2 Two components of the shock
sections.text: Let S ¯ H ​ ( ℓ , h ) \bar{S}^{H}(\ell,h) be the human call probability averaged over contexts. The change in the call probability for a given pitch decomposes into S M ​ ( ℓ , h ) − S H ​ ( ℓ , h , θ ) = [ S M ​ ( ℓ , h ) − S ¯ H ​ ( ℓ , h ) ] ⏟ geometric − [ S H ​ ( ℓ , h , θ ) − S ¯ H ​ ( ℓ , h ) ] ⏟ discretionary . S^{M}(\ell,h)-S^{H}(\ell,h,\theta)=\underbrace{\big[S^{M}(\ell,h)-\bar{S}^{H}(\ell,h)\big]}_{\text{geometric}}-\underbrace{\big[S^{H}(\ell,h,\theta)-\bar{S}^{H}(\ell,h)\big]}_{\text{discretionary}}. (2) The geometric component reflects the difference between the rule’s zone and the human zone. It varies only with location, height and handedness, and it is a redistribution chosen by the rule’s designers. The discretionary component is the part of human judgment that responds to context, and the machine sets it to zero. It is a set of rents created by the human evaluator: deference to stars, adjustments to the count, and the value of a catcher’s ability to influence calls.

sections.heading: 2.3 Hypotheses
sections.text: Our first hypothesis, H1, is that the machine removes discretion. Holding location fixed, called-strike probabilities under the ABS do not depend on the count, the batter’s reputation or the catcher. The pre-ABS size of each context effect measures a rent that the machine removes. Catcher framing is a skill whose value comes from the evaluator’s errors, so it should be a persistent catcher attribute before the ABS and indistinguishable from noise after it. The second hypothesis, H2, is that the geometric incidence of the change follows the rule’s design. Because Z ⁡ ( h ) Z(h) scales with registered height and is symmetric across handedness, the ABS shifts strikes toward tall batters at the top of the zone. It also removes any handedness asymmetry in the human zone. The third hypothesis, H3, is that the economic incidence of the change equals exposure times price. To first order, the change in a batter’s expected plate-appearance value is Δ V ≈ − ∑ taken pitches Δ S ( ℓ , h , θ ) Δ v ( θ ) = − E × Δ ​ v ¯ , \Delta V\;\approx\;-\sum_{\text{taken pitches}}\Delta S(\ell,h,\theta)\,\Delta v(\theta)\;=\;-E\times\overline{\Delta v}, (3) where E E is the number of calls per plate appearance that the shock flips. Large changes in call probabilities therefore translate into small changes in outcomes when the affected pitches are rare. Where we observe an outcome change for a group, the call channel in ( 3 ) bounds the part of that change attributable to the ABS. The fourth hypothesis, H4, concerns pitchers, who should reallocate their pitches toward locations whose value rose, with partial adjustment. We divide the plate into five vertical bands (the three thirds of the ABS zone and the areas above and below it) and five horizontal bands (the three thirds of its width and the areas beyond each side). A cell c c is a pitch type (fastball, slider, curveball and so on) in one of the 25 resulting areas, and s t ​ ( c ) s_{t}(c) is the share of that pitch type’s pitches thrown to the area in season t t . The ABS changes the value of cell c c by its mechanical shock G ⁡ ( c ) G(c) , the change in the cell’s value to the pitcher, in wOBA points per 1,000 pitches, when its 2022–2023 called pitches are re-judged by the ABS rule with behavior held fixed. We model usage as partial adjustment toward a target, the reduced form implied by convex adjustment costs ( Lucas, 1967 ; Gould, 1968 ) : Δ ​ s t ​ ( c ) = λ ⁡ [ s t ∗ ​ ( c ) − s t − 1 ​ ( c ) ] , s 2024 ∗ ​ ( c ) − s 2023 ∗ ​ ( c ) = κ ​ G ​ ( c ) . \Delta s_{t}(c)=\lambda\,\big[s^{*}_{t}(c)-s_{t-1}(c)\big],\qquad s^{*}_{2024}(c)-s^{*}_{2023}(c)=\kappa\,G(c). (4) Three implications follow. First, the 2024 change in usage responds to G G over and above any pre-existing trend: if β t \beta_{t} denotes the slope of the usage change on G G in season t t , the acceleration A = β 2024 − β 2023 A=\beta_{2024}-\beta_{2023} is positive. Second, the response fades once the new target is reached, so β 2025 \beta_{2025} and β 2026 \beta_{2026} are close to zero; a small negative value would indicate overshooting followed by correction. Third, groups that were already moving toward the new target before 2024 show little acceleration, whereas groups that had not moved catch up. These implications require only that usage move in proportion to its distance from the target, not that it move slowly; they hold for any adjustment speed λ \lambda , including one close to one. The fifth hypothesis, H5, is that agents re-optimize only when the gain exceeds the cost. Even professionals can leave sizable gains unexploited ( Romer, 2006 ) , which suggests that changing a strategy is costly. Suppose that changing a decision rule carries a fixed cognitive or practice cost in addition to the convex cost above, as in models that combine the two ( Cooper and Haltiwanger, 2006 ) . An agent then adjusts only when the expected gain exceeds the fixed cost, so that adjustment is lumpy ( Caballero and Engel, 1999 ) , and the convex cost governs how quickly an agent that does adjust approaches its target. The two sides of the plate face different gains. A pitcher’s location plan is set in advance and applies to every batter, so its gain scales with the league-wide movement of the zone. A batter’s swing decision is made in a fraction of a second, and its gain scales with the batter’s own exposure E E , which H3 implies is small. We therefore expect pitchers to adapt and batters not to, even after the count stops affecting calls.

sections.heading: 3.1 The ABS in the KBO
sections.text: Since the start of the 2024 season the KBO has used the ABS in every regular-season game. A tracking system measures every pitch, and a strike-determination system relays the call to the umpire through an earpiece. Calls cannot be challenged. The rule defines the zone relative to each batter’s registered height. In 2024 the bottom and top of the zone were 27.64% and 56.35% of height. From 2025 both bounds moved down by 0.6 percentage points, to 27.04% and 55.75%, and they were unchanged in 2026. Horizontally, the zone is the plate widened by 2 cm on each side, 47.18 cm in total. According to the league’s rules, the horizontal bounds are checked at the middle plane of the plate, and a strike requires the pitch to meet the vertical bounds at both the middle plane and the back plane ( Korea Baseball Organization, 2026 ) . The published rules do not say whether a pitch that only partly overlaps the zone is a strike. Three other rule changes overlap with our sample. In 2024 the league limited defensive shifts (moving infielders toward the side of the field to which a batter tends to hit) and enlarged the bases; a pitch clock (a time limit between pitches) was piloted in the same year, adopted in 2025 and relaxed in 2026; and in 2022, two years before the ABS, the league instructed umpires to call a wider zone. None of these changes enters the call function S S , so tests based on calls are unaffected by them. Tests based on behavior and outcomes rely on contrasts within the league, by height, handedness, exposure and pitching arm, so that league-wide shocks are absorbed by season fixed effects.

sections.heading: 3.2 Pitch-level data
sections.text: We collect every regular-season pitch from 2021 to 2026 from the play-by-play feed of Naver Sports, the sports service of the Korean web portal Naver, which publishes the league’s tracking data ( Naver Sports, 2026 ) . For each pitch we observe the call or batted-ball outcome, the pitch type and velocity, and the nine parameters of the fitted trajectory. We also observe the batter’s registered height and batting side (left or right), the pitcher’s throwing arm, and the result of the plate appearance. We add the four umpires listed for each game and the catcher on the field for each pitch, which we reconstruct from the starting lineup and the substitution log. We restrict the sample to April–September, so that each season covers the same months, and drop the All-Star Game. The final sample contains 1,203,755 pitches, of which 657,201 were called, and 308,959 plate appearances. Table 1 summarizes them by season. Among other statistics, it reports the share of high pitches, those in the upper third of the ABS zone or above (the top two of the five vertical bands defined in Section 2 ). The seasons play different roles. The two seasons 2022–2023 form the human-umpire baseline, and every quantity defined relative to the human zone is estimated on them alone. The most important is the human zone itself, S ¯ H ​ ( x , z ) \bar{S}^{H}(x,z) , the probability of a called strike at horizontal position x x and height above the ground z z . We estimate it from 2022–2023 calls with a logit model in which this probability is a smooth function of x x and z z (a generalized additive model with a tensor-product spline). Because z z is measured in absolute terms, the estimated zone is free to ignore the batter’s height. Treating the human zone as a smooth probability of a strike, rather than a sharp boundary, follows the evidence that umpires’ calls behave like a psychophysical judgment that becomes less certain near the edge ( Flannagan et al., 2024 ) . The count values v v and the mechanical shocks G G are also estimated on these two seasons. The seasons 2024–2026 are the ABS seasons. We use 2021 only for pre-trend tests: it precedes the 2022 zone expansion, and the season was interrupted by COVID-19 and resumed without extra innings (the additional innings played when a game is tied after nine).

sections.heading: 3.3 Reconstructing locations and the ABS rule
sections.text: We compute the location at which each pitch crosses the plate from its fitted trajectory and express its height as a fraction of the batter’s registered height, z / h z/h , the unit in which the ABS zone is defined. Because the published rules leave some details open, Appendix Table A1 searches over candidate definitions and compares each with the 2024–2026 ABS calls. Two features matter. Calls match far better when a strike requires only that some part of the ball touch the zone, as Lee et al. (2025) assume, than when the whole ball must be inside it (98.6% against 93.0%), and the 2 cm widening adds two percentage points. The choice of plane matters little: checking the vertical bounds at the middle plane alone or, as the rules state, at both the middle and the back plane gives 98.6% and 98.5%. We use the middle plane alone, which fits marginally better and gives each pitch a single location. This rule reproduces 98.6% of calls using registered heights, and 99.1% using the height list the system itself applies, which we back out from the tracking data’s zone bounds (Appendix Tables A3 and A4 ). Applied to the human-umpire seasons, the same reconstruction agrees with 91.4% and 91.6% of calls in 2022 and 2023; most of the disagreements are balls called inside the zone. Two measurement issues require attention. The first is a change in the source format: from games on 16 July 2026 the source data report trajectories relative to a reference point 55 ft from the plate instead of 50 ft. Ignoring this would inflate plate-crossing heights by 12–19 cm. After the correction, the replication rate is identical before and after the switch (Appendix Table A3 ). The second is the stability of the tracking calibration, since a recalibration of the vertical axis could masquerade as pitchers throwing higher. Within a pitcher and pitch type, the height of the ball 50 ft from the plate, close to the release point (where the ball leaves the pitcher’s hand), changes by at most 1.8 cm across seasons (Appendix Table A2 ). This is small relative to the changes in plate-crossing height that we attribute to behavior.

sections.heading: 4 Empirical Strategy
sections.text: The ABS was introduced in every game at once, so no part of the league remained under human umpires after 2024. Our designs therefore exploit variation in how strongly the change in the call function bears on different pitches, players and locations, and they lean on the fact that the call function itself is untouched by the league’s other rule changes. This section describes each design and the assumption under which it identifies the effect of the ABS. Regressions of binary outcomes are linear probability models. Because we test many hypotheses, we also compute, within the family of tests reported in each table, q q -values adjusted for the false discovery rate with the procedure of Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) .

sections.heading: 4.1 Calls
sections.text: To locate the change in the call function, we divide called pitches into eight regions defined relative to the 2024 ABS zone and the batter’s registered height: the three thirds of the zone; the high and low edges, bands just above and below the zone; the inside and outside edges, bands just beyond the side of the zone nearer to and farther from the batter; and everything farther out. For a called pitch i i in region r r , thrown by pitcher p p to batter b b in month m m of season t t , we estimate Strike i = α r + δ r ​ ABS t + μ p + μ b + μ m + ε i , \text{Strike}_{i}=\alpha_{r}+\delta_{r}\,\text{ABS}_{t}+\mu_{p}+\mu_{b}+\mu_{m}+\varepsilon_{i}, (5) where Strike i \text{Strike}_{i} indicates a called strike, ABS t \text{ABS}_{t} indicates the 2024–2026 seasons, and μ p \mu_{p} , μ b \mu_{b} and μ m \mu_{m} are pitcher, batter and month fixed effects. The coefficient δ r \delta_{r} is the change in the probability that a pitch in region r r is called a strike after the machine replaced the umpire, holding the pitcher and the batter fixed. Standard errors in this and every other regression of calls are clustered by game, because pitches in the same game share an umpire, a ballpark and conditions. This is a before–after comparison within a region, and δ r \delta_{r} measures the effect of the ABS under the assumption that, absent the machine, the probability that a pitch in region r r thrown by a given pitcher to a given batter is called a strike would have stayed at its 2022–2023 level. Because the limits on defensive shifts, the larger bases and the pitch clock do not enter the call, these other changes cannot violate the assumption. It would fail if human umpires were already changing their calls, which we check by replacing ABS t \text{ABS}_{t} with indicators for each season from 2021 to 2026, with 2023 as the reference. The ABS rule treats every pitcher–batter matchup identically. To ask whether human umpires did, we estimate equation ( 5 ) separately for each combination of pitching arm and batting side. Raw call rates could differ across matchups simply because pitches land in different parts of an edge, so we also modify equation ( 5 ) to compare pitches at the same location. For each side edge (inside and outside) and each period (2022–2023 and 2024–2026), we replace the regressors of equation ( 5 ) with indicators for three matchups, whose coefficients we denote γ k \gamma_{k} , and with fixed effects μ ℓ \mu_{\ell} for the fine location bin ℓ \ell of the pitch, 3 cm horizontally by 2% of the batter’s height vertically. The three matchups are right-handed pitchers facing left-handed batters and left-handed pitchers facing right- and left-handed batters, with right-handed pitchers facing right-handed batters as the reference. Each γ k \gamma_{k} is then the difference in the called-strike probability between matchup k k and the reference matchup at the same location, and a Wald F F -test of γ 1 = γ 2 = γ 3 = 0 \gamma_{1}=\gamma_{2}=\gamma_{3}=0 asks whether all four matchups are called alike. A rule that is symmetric across handedness implies that this null holds under the ABS. To measure how much the change in calls matters for plate appearances, we compute the exposure E E in equation ( 3 ) directly. We re-judge every 2022–2023 called pitch with the ABS rule, holding behavior fixed, and count for each plate appearance the strikes the ABS would have added: pitches inside the ABS zone that umpires called balls, minus pitches outside it that umpires called strikes. Averaging this count over the plate appearances of each matchup gives E E . This is a calculation rather than an estimate. The discretionary component is identified by difference-in-differences on border pitches , the called pitches within 0.18 ft (5.5 cm, about one and a half ball widths) of the ABS zone boundary, where context can plausibly sway a human call: Y i = β 1 ​ X i + β 2 ​ X i × ABS t + μ ℓ ​ t + μ p + μ u + ε i , Y_{i}=\beta_{1}X_{i}+\beta_{2}\,X_{i}\times\text{ABS}_{t}+\mu_{\ell t}+\mu_{p}+\mu_{u}+\varepsilon_{i}, (6) where Y i = Strike i Y_{i}=\text{Strike}_{i} , X i X_{i} is a context variable, μ ℓ ​ t \mu_{\ell t} are fixed effects for location bins interacted with season, and μ u \mu_{u} are fixed effects for the home-plate umpire u u . We consider three contexts. Following the evidence that status affects umpires’ calls ( Kim and King, 2014 ) , we define a star batter as one whose on-base percentage (the share of plate appearances in which the batter reaches base by a hit, a walk or being hit by a pitch) was in the top 20% among batters with at least 300 plate appearances in the previous season. The second context is whether the batter plays for the home team. The third is the count, grouped into hitter-ahead counts (2-0, 3-0 and 3-1), two-strike counts, and all other counts as the reference. The specifications for the home team and the count add batter fixed effects μ b \mu_{b} . For star status we report the estimate with and without them; with them, β 2 \beta_{2} is identified from batters whose status changes. The coefficient β 1 \beta_{1} is the human umpires’ context effect at a given location, and β 2 \beta_{2} is its change under the ABS. The identifying assumption is that, absent the ABS, the gap in calls between contexts at the same location would have remained constant. We assess it for star status by replacing β 1 ​ X i + β 2 ​ X i × ABS t \beta_{1}X_{i}+\beta_{2}X_{i}\times\text{ABS}_{t} with a separate coefficient on X i X_{i} for each season, which shows whether the gap was stable before 2024. Equation ( 6 ) also serves as the template for several designs below, which change the outcome Y i Y_{i} , the regressors and the fixed effects. To measure catcher framing, we adapt equation ( 6 ). For each season separately and on all called pitches, we replace β 1 ​ X i + β 2 ​ X i × ABS t \beta_{1}X_{i}+\beta_{2}X_{i}\times\text{ABS}_{t} with a fixed effect ϕ j \phi_{j} for the catcher j j who received the pitch, and use fixed effects for location bin, pitcher, batter and home-plate umpire. Because catchers on the same team share pitchers, ϕ j \phi_{j} is identified only relative to teammates, so we normalize the effects to have a pitch-weighted mean of zero within each team and keep catchers with at least 1,500 called pitches. We measure the persistence of framing in two ways: the split-half reliability, the correlation between ϕ j \phi_{j} estimated on alternating games of the same season, and the correlation between a catcher’s ϕ j \phi_{j} in consecutive seasons. Each correlation is tested against zero with the t t -test for a Pearson correlation, which has n − 2 n-2 degrees of freedom for n n catchers. To value framing in runs, we multiply each catcher’s effect by the catcher’s number of called pitches and by the run value of a strike, and take the standard deviation across catchers.

sections.heading: 4.2 Pitchers
sections.text: For pitchers we cannot compare treated and untreated groups, because every pitcher faced the machine. Instead we use the fact that the ABS changed the value of some locations much more than others. For each cell c c defined in Section 2 (a pitch type in one of 25 areas of the plate) with at least 150 pitches in 2022–2023, we compute its mechanical shock G ⁡ ( c ) G(c) from 2022–2023 pitches alone, and estimate for each season s t ​ ( c ) − s t − 1 ​ ( c ) = a f + β t ​ G ​ ( c ) + e c , t , s_{t}(c)-s_{t-1}(c)=a_{f}+\beta_{t}\,G(c)+e_{c,t}, (7) where s t ​ ( c ) s_{t}(c) is the cell’s share, in percent, of its pitch type’s pitches, a f a_{f} are fixed effects for the pitch type f f of cell c c , and cells are weighted by their baseline pitches. This is a continuous-treatment difference-in-differences across cells, with G G as the treatment intensity. A positive β 2024 \beta_{2024} alone does not identify a response to the ABS, because usage may already have been drifting toward cells that the ABS later favored. We therefore focus on the acceleration A = β 2024 − β 2023 A=\beta_{2024}-\beta_{2023} , which we estimate by regressing the difference between the 2024 and 2023 changes in usage on G G in the same way. It identifies the effect under the assumption that, absent the ABS, the drift would have continued at its 2023 pace. Two checks support the assumption. The slope for 2022 provides a placebo, and, for groups whose 2023 slope is zero, the acceleration reduces to the 2024 slope. To ask whether pitchers did more than move their pitches up or down, we also estimate A A with fixed effects for the five vertical bands, which compares cells at the same height. We estimate these slopes for all pitchers, separately by pitching arm, and in a balanced panel of pitchers with at least 300 pitches in at least three seasons. Because cells pool the pitches of many pitchers, we compute standard errors from 999 bootstrap replications that resample pitchers and test the slopes with z z -tests. To compare the timing of the move toward high pitches across pitching arms, we regress each pitcher’s share of high pitches in a season on pitcher fixed effects and season indicators, with 2023 as the reference. We estimate this regression in the balanced panel, separately for left-handed, right-handed and side-arm pitchers, weighting by pitches and clustering standard errors by pitcher. Each season coefficient θ s \theta_{s} is the within-pitcher change in the high-pitch share between season s s and 2023. To ask whether human umpires treated high pitches differently by pitching arm before the ABS, we adapt equation ( 6 ) once more, estimating it on called pitches in the upper third of the zone and the high edge in 2022–2023. Its regressors are the interactions of indicators for left-handed and side-arm pitchers with an indicator for 2022, with right-handed pitchers as the reference, and its fixed effects are for location bin, season, pitching arm and batter. The coefficient λ a \lambda_{a} on each interaction is the change in the called-strike probability from 2023 to 2022 for arm a a relative to right-handed pitchers at the same location.

sections.heading: 4.3 Batters
sections.text: The ABS scales the zone with registered height, so height determines how strongly the geometric shock bears on a batter. We measure the shock with each batter-season’s excess strike rate on high pitches, D b ​ t D_{bt} . For each high pitch within 1 ft of the center of the plate that batter b b took in season t t , we subtract from the actual call (one for a strike, zero for a ball) the probability that the 2022–2023 human zone would have called it a strike, and D b ​ t D_{bt} is the average of these differences. For batters observed both before and after the ABS, we estimate D b ​ t = α b + τ t + π ⁡ ( h b − h ¯ ) × ABS t + u b ​ t , D_{bt}=\alpha_{b}+\tau_{t}+\pi\,(h_{b}-\bar{h})\times\text{ABS}_{t}+u_{bt}, (8) where h b h_{b} is registered height, h ¯ = 182 \bar{h}=182 cm, α b \alpha_{b} and τ t \tau_{t} are batter and season fixed effects, and batter-seasons are weighted by their number of high pitches. This is the first stage. It is a continuous-treatment difference-in-differences with height as the treatment intensity, and the identifying assumption is parallel trends across heights. We examine the assumption by replacing ( h b − h ¯ ) × ABS t (h_{b}-\bar{h})\times\text{ABS}_{t} with ( h b − h ¯ ) (h_{b}-\bar{h}) interacted with each season from 2021 to 2026, relative to 2023. Taller batters hit more home runs and strike out more (Appendix Table A6 ), but batter fixed effects absorb such level differences, and the assumption requires only that their trends do not differ. Standard errors in all regressions for batters are clustered by batter, except where noted. The reduced form replaces D b ​ t D_{bt} in equation ( 8 ) with the batter’s behavior and plate-appearance outcomes, at the level of the pitch or the plate appearance, keeping π ⁡ ( h b − h ¯ ) × ABS t \pi\,(h_{b}-\bar{h})\times\text{ABS}_{t} and batter fixed effects. When the outcome is whether a pitch is high, we add fixed effects for pitcher by season and for count by season. When it is whether the batter swings at a pitch in the area the ABS added to the zone (above the top of the human zone, 3.35 ft, and inside the ABS zone), we add fixed effects for absolute location bins (3 cm by 3 cm) by season, for count by season, and for pitcher. When it is whether a plate appearance reaches two strikes or three balls, we add fixed effects for pitcher by season. To test whether batters responded to the end of count-dependent calls, we extend equation ( 6 ) to a triple difference, estimated on border pitches and pitches in the heart of the zone (inside the zone and more than 0.18 ft from its boundary). The outcome Y i Y_{i} is an indicator for a swing, and the regressors are Border i × ABS t \text{Border}_{i}\times\text{ABS}_{t} and its interactions with the hitter-ahead and two-strike count groups, with other counts as the reference. The fixed effects are for location bin by season, count group by season, count group by border, pitcher and batter, and standard errors are clustered by game. The coefficient ψ g \psi_{g} on the triple interaction for count group g g is the change under the ABS in the difference in swing rates between border and heart pitches in that count group, relative to other counts. Calls in the heart of the zone did not depend on the count even under human umpires, so they absorb any change in swing behavior by count that is unrelated to the calls. As a placebo, we estimate the same regression on 2022–2023 with 2023 treated as if it were the first ABS season. Finally, we estimate equation ( 6 ) at the plate-appearance level for star batters over 2022–2026. The outcome Y i Y_{i} indicates a walk, a strikeout or reaching base, or is the plate-appearance value; X i X_{i} is star status; and the fixed effects are for batter and for pitcher by season. We denote its coefficients ρ 1 \rho_{1} and ρ 2 \rho_{2} , so that ρ 2 \rho_{2} is the change in star batters’ outcomes under the ABS. We compare ρ 2 \rho_{2} for the plate-appearance value with the change that the call channel in equation ( 3 ) predicts. The prediction multiplies the pre-ABS star coefficient β 1 \beta_{1} from the call regression by the value Δ ​ v \Delta v of each border pitch that star batters took in 2022–2023, sums over these pitches, and divides by star batters’ plate appearances in the same seasons. Treating the prediction as fixed, we test whether ρ 2 \rho_{2} equals it with a t t -test. To express the call channel in runs per season, we multiply it by 550 plate appearances and divide by the wOBA scale of 1.2. Because earlier work uses 2023 alone as the pre-ABS season, we also estimate this regression with that baseline.

sections.heading: 5 Results
sections.text: We present the results in three steps. We first characterize what the machine changed in the call function, separating its geometric and discretionary components (H1–H2). We then study how pitchers reallocated their pitches (H4), and finally ask whether batters bore the incidence of the change and whether they responded to it (H3, H5).

sections.heading: 5.1 Calls: geometry and discretion
sections.text: Our reconstruction of the ABS rule reproduces 98.6% of ABS calls in 2024 and 98.6% in 2026, against 91.4% and 91.6% of human calls in 2022 and 2023 (Table 1 ). The overall called-strike rate barely changed. The zone did not grow but moved (Appendix Figure A1 ), as Lee et al. (2025) document for the first half of 2024. Table 2 asks where on the plate the calls changed and whether the change follows the rule’s geometry. Panel A reports δ r \delta_{r} from equation ( 5 ) for each of the eight regions. Every δ r \delta_{r} is significantly different from zero at the 1% level, and the signs follow the rule. A pitch in the upper third of the zone became 13.9 percentage points more likely to be called a strike, because human umpires had called a seventh of these pitches balls. A pitch in the band just below the zone became − 15.2 -15.2 points less likely to be a strike, because human umpires had called a third of them strikes. Pitches in the middle of the zone, already called strikes 95% of the time, changed little. The season-by-season estimates of equation ( 5 ) in Appendix Table A9 show that the change at the top of the zone and on the inside edge arrived in 2024, after two stable human-umpire seasons. On the outside edge and below the zone, by contrast, human calls were already moving in the same direction between 2022 and 2023, so the before–after estimates overstate the effect of the machine there; relative to 2023 alone, the change is − 3.2 -3.2 points on the outside edge and − 18.5 -18.5 points below the zone. The within-pitcher coefficients θ s \theta_{s} (Figure 2 b) show that right-handed and side-arm pitchers were already raising their pitches between 2021 and 2023, whereas left-handed pitchers were flat until the ABS arrived. The relationship between the shock and the change in usage is flat for left-handed pitchers before the ABS and steep after it, but similar in both periods for right-handed pitchers.

sections.heading: 5.4 Robustness
sections.text: Appendix Table A7 re-estimates the main coefficients under alternative specifications. For the calls, we narrow or widen the border band to 0.12 or 0.25 ft, coarsen or refine the location bins to 6 or 1.5 cm, estimate a logit instead of a linear probability model, define star status by the top 10% or 30% of on-base percentage or fix it at its 2021 value, and drop 2026. For pitchers, we require 100 or 300 instead of 150 baseline pitches per cell, and for batters we drop 2026. The removal of count-dependent calls is robust to every change. The left-handed pitchers’ acceleration is equally stable when we change the minimum number of baseline pitches per cell, and the first stage and the null reduced form for batters are unchanged without 2026. The removal of the star advantage is less robust. It survives a narrower or wider border band, finer location bins, a broader definition of star status (the top 30% of on-base percentage) and the exclusion of 2026. It shrinks and loses significance, however, when location bins are coarsened to 6 cm, when the model is a logit, and when star status is restricted to the top 10%, and it is significant only at the 10% level when status is fixed at its 2021 value. The logit is informative here: once the ABS makes calls a deterministic function of location, many location bins are perfectly predicted after 2024 and drop out of the logit, so it identifies the interaction from a different and smaller set of pitches. We read the evidence as showing that human umpires favored star batters on border pitches, but that the size of the effect depends on how finely location is held fixed. Appendix Table A8 reports the false-discovery-rate adjusted q q -values. The removal of the star advantage ( q = 0.004 q=0.004 ), the removal of count-dependent calls ( q < 0.001 q<0.001 ) and the acceleration of left-handed pitchers ( q < 0.001 q<0.001 ) survive the adjustment. The two marginal results for batters do not: the increase in star batters’ strikeouts ( q = 0.27 q=0.27 ) and the response of two-strike swings ( q = 0.33 q=0.33 ). This reinforces our reading that we cannot detect changes in batters’ behavior or outcomes.

sections.heading: 5.5 Summary
sections.text: The machine removed three rents created by human judgment: deference to star batters, adjustments to the count, and the value of catcher framing (H1). It also redistributed strikes along two geometric margins chosen by its designers, height and handedness (H2). The redistribution was large in terms of call probabilities but small in terms of plate-appearance outcomes, because few pitches are exposed to it (H3). Pitchers re-optimized quickly and coarsely, and the group that had not already moved caught up (H4). We find no detectable response by batters, either to the new geometry or to the end of count-dependent calls (H5).

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper studies what happens when an algorithm replaces human judgment in a setting where every decision is recorded and the quality of each decision can be measured. In 2024 the KBO replaced the home-plate umpire’s ball–strike judgment with an automated system, and we follow more than a million pitches from 2021 to 2026 to trace the consequences for the evaluator’s calls, for the pitchers who throw the pitches, and for the batters who face them. The machine changed the call function in two distinct ways. It removed the discretionary component of human judgment. Before 2024, umpires expanded the zone when the batter was ahead in the count and contracted it with two strikes. Their calls depended on the catcher in a way that was stable within and across seasons, and they gave star batters slightly more benefit of the doubt on border pitches, although the size of this last effect depends on how finely location is held fixed. None of the three patterns is detectable under the ABS. At the same time, the machine imposed a geometry chosen by the rule’s designers. Because the human zone was anchored in absolute height and the machine’s zone scales with registered height, strikes moved toward taller batters at the top of the zone. Because human umpires treated matchups asymmetrically and the machine does not, strikes moved between right- and left-handed matchups at the edges. These changes were large in terms of call probabilities but small in terms of outcomes. A pitch in the upper third of the zone became 13.9 percentage points more likely to be called a strike. Yet the extra strikes amount to at most one in every 23 plate appearances for the most exposed matchup, and ten centimeters of height change the probability that a plate appearance reaches two strikes or three balls by less than two percentage points. The value of catcher framing and of the star advantage was real, but it amounted to a few runs per catcher-season and about one run per star batter-season. This suggests that the incidence of a change in an evaluation rule may depend on exposure as much as on the size of the change: a rule can move decisions sharply at the margin while leaving the distribution of outcomes nearly intact, because few cases sit at the margin. The two sides of the plate responded very differently. Pitchers reallocated their pitches toward the locations that the machine made more valuable, and they did so quickly and coarsely. The response was concentrated in the first season, worked almost entirely through pitch height rather than pitch type or side of the plate, and was partly unwound in the third season. Left-handed pitchers, who had not taken part in the league’s earlier drift toward high pitches, account for the acceleration at the time of the ABS and converged to the other groups within a season. Batters, by contrast, show no detectable change in their swing decisions, either in response to the new geometry or to the end of count-dependent calls, even though the value of taking a border pitch changed substantially in some counts. This asymmetry is consistent with a simple cost of re-optimization. A pitcher’s plan applies to every batter and is set in advance, so its gain scales with the league-wide shift in the zone, whereas a batter’s decision is made in real time and its gain scales with the batter’s own small exposure. The findings bear on the design of automated evaluation in sport and beyond. Leagues that adopt automated calls, fully or through challenge systems such as those used in tennis and, since 2026, in Major League Baseball ( Abramitzky et al., 2012 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , choose a geometry when they write the rule, and that choice shapes who gains and who loses. Scaling the zone with height, defining the plane at which the ball is judged, and widening the plate are design parameters with distributional consequences, not technical details. More generally, our results suggest that replacing a human evaluator with a rule can eliminate the rents that the evaluator’s discretion created, including the value of skills whose purpose was to influence that discretion, but need not by itself make outcomes more equal across agents. The incidence of the new rule is likely to depend on its geometry and on how many cases it touches. Several limitations qualify these conclusions. We observe one league and three seasons after the change, so we cannot say whether batters eventually adapt or whether the partial reversal in pitchers’ behavior in 2026 persists. We do not observe salaries or contracts, so the labor-market consequences of the rents we document remain open. Our measure of star status relies on past on-base percentage, which captures reputation imperfectly. Our pitch locations come from the league’s tracking data; we validate their stability within pitchers and against the system’s own calls, but we cannot verify the pre-2024 coordinates independently. Finally, our analyses of behavior and outcomes rely on contrasts within the league to absorb the other rule changes of 2024–2026, an assumption that the calls themselves do not need. Comparisons with leagues that kept human umpires, and with Major League Baseball’s challenge system, in which umpires still make every call but players can ask the machine to overturn some of them ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , would sharpen these results.

Evidence from the Automated Ball-Strike System (ABS) Abstract In 2024 the Korea Baseball Organization became the first top-tier league to replace the home-plate umpire’s ball–strike judgment with an automated system. Using over a million pitches from 2021 to 2026, we separate the change into the removal of human discretion and the imposition of a new zone geometry. The machine eliminated count-dependent calls, the value of catcher framing and a small advantage for star batters, rents worth only a few runs per player-season. Because the machine’s zone scales with height and treats every matchup alike, it redistributed strikes toward tall batters and across matchups; but few pitches are exposed to these changes, and their effects on plate-appearance outcomes are precisely estimated and close to zero. Pitchers re-optimized quickly by throwing higher, with left-handers catching up to an existing trend, whereas we find no evidence that batters adjusted. The results suggest that the incidence of replacing human judgment with a rule depends on its geometry and on exposure. Keywords: automated ball-strike system; algorithmic decision-making; evaluator bias; rents; adaptation JEL classification: Z22, J24, D83, O33 1 Introduction Algorithms increasingly replace human judgment in decisions about people, from hiring and lending to bail and grading. A large literature asks whether such algorithms decide better than the humans they replace ( Kleinberg et al., 2018 ; Hoffman et al., 2018 ) . Less is known about what the replacement does to the people being evaluated. Removing human discretion should eliminate the advantages that discretion created, but a rule also has a shape. The shape determines who gains and who loses, and those affected may or may not change their behavior in response. Answering these questions requires a setting in which every decision is recorded, the rule that replaces human judgment is known, and the behavior of those being evaluated can be observed before and after the change. Professional baseball offers such a setting. Every pitch is tracked, every ball–strike call (the umpire’s ruling on a pitch the batter does not swing at) is recorded, and the call is the outcome of a judgment that, until recently, was made by a human umpire. In 2024 the Korea Baseball Organization (KBO) became the first top-tier professional league to hand that judgment entirely to an automated ball-strike system (ABS). The ABS calls a strike whenever any part of the ball passes through a rectangle defined by each batter’s registered height. We study this change using every regular-season pitch thrown in the KBO from 2021 to 2026, more than a million pitches. We combine the pitches with the tracking system’s trajectories, the umpires assigned to each game, and the catcher on the field for each pitch. We organize the analysis around a simple decomposition. Relative to a human umpire, the machine changes calls in two ways. It removes the discretionary component of human judgment, that is, the part of the call that responds to context such as the count (the number of balls and strikes so far in the plate appearance), the batter’s reputation or the catcher’s receiving skill. It also imposes a new geometry , the difference between the zone the rule defines and the zone humans actually called. The first component is a set of rents created by the evaluator; the second is a redistribution chosen by the rule’s designers. To a first approximation, the economic incidence of either component equals the number of calls it changes per plate appearance (a batter’s turn at bat) times the value of a ball relative to a strike. Finally, those affected should adapt only when the gain from adapting exceeds its cost. Three sets of findings emerge. First, the machine removed the rents created by human discretion. On border pitches, those close to the edge of the zone, human umpires were 6.1 percentage points more likely to call a strike when the batter was ahead in the count (2-0, 3-0 or 3-1) and 6.7 points less likely with two strikes; neither adjustment is detectable under the ABS. Catcher framing, the skill of receiving pitches so that umpires call them strikes, was persistent under human umpires, with split-half reliabilities between 0.60 and 0.81, and it became indistinguishable from noise under the machine. Human umpires also gave star batters slightly fewer called strikes on border pitches, although the size of this effect depends on how finely location is held fixed. Valued at what a strike costs the batting team in expected runs, these rents amounted to a few runs per catcher-season and about one run per star batter-season. Second, the geometry of the rule redistributed strikes along two margins, but the redistribution had little effect on outcomes. Because the human zone was anchored in absolute height while the machine’s zone scales with registered height, the ABS moved strikes toward taller batters at the top of the zone: relative to the human zone, each centimeter of height added 0.75 percentage points to the share of a batter’s high pitches that were called strikes. Because human umpires treated pitcher–batter matchups asymmetrically, the machine also moved strikes between handedness matchups at the edges. Few pitches are exposed to these changes, however. The extra strikes amount to at most one in every 23 plate appearances, and ten centimeters of height change the probability that a plate appearance reaches two strikes or three balls, one call away from a strikeout or a walk, by less than two percentage points. Third, pitchers adapted and batters did not. Using the change in each location’s value under the machine as a measure of treatment intensity, we find that pitchers reallocated their pitches toward locations the ABS favored, quickly and almost entirely through pitch height. The acceleration at the time of the ABS comes from left-handed pitchers. Right-handed and side-arm pitchers (those who throw with a low, sideways arm angle) had already been raising their pitches before 2024, whereas left-handed pitchers had not, and they caught up within a season. For batters, by contrast, we detect no change in swing decisions, either in response to the new geometry or to the end of count-dependent calls. This asymmetry is consistent with a simple cost of re-optimization. A pitcher’s plan is set in advance and applies to every batter, whereas a batter decides in real time, and the stakes for any one batter are small. The paper contributes to four literatures. A body of work in economics and management documents that human evaluators in sport are influenced by race ( Price and Wolfers, 2010 ; Parsons et al., 2011 ; Tainsky et al., 2015 ; Hamrick and Rasp, 2015 ) , status ( Kim and King, 2014 ; Mills, 2014 ) , nationality ( Zitzewitz, 2006 ) , the sequence of past decisions ( Chen et al., 2016 ) , the count ( MacMahon and Starkes, 2008 ) , and the home crowd ( Sutter and Kocher, 2004 ; Garicano et al., 2005 ; Dohmen, 2008 ; Hsu, 2024 ) , and that the quality of their judgment varies with working conditions ( Fesselmeyer, 2021 ) . A related set of studies shows that these biases respond to the evaluator’s environment: favoritism fell when referees became full-time professionals ( Rickman and Witt, 2008 ) and when referees became aware of their bias ( Pope et al., 2018 ) , and pitch-tracking technology changed how umpires called the zone ( Mills, 2017 ; Hunter, 2018 ; Bradbury, 2019 ) . These studies observe human evaluators under different incentives and degrees of scrutiny. We observe the complete replacement of the evaluator, which allows us to measure the rents that discretion created and to test whether they vanish. Our results also relate to the economics of algorithmic decision-making ( Kleinberg et al., 2018 ; Hoffman et al., 2018 ) . That literature compares the quality of human and machine decisions. We show that the distributional consequences of replacing humans with a rule are governed by the rule’s geometry and by exposure, and that those evaluated by the rule may not adapt to it. Third, we add to the evidence on how professional agents adjust their strategies when payoffs change. Some studies find that professionals play close to optimally ( Walker and Wooders, 2001 ; Chiappori et al., 2002 ; Palacios-Huerta, 2003 ; Abramitzky et al., 2012 ) and change their strategies as theory predicts when the rules change ( Banerjee et al., 2007 ) , while others document persistent departures from optimal play ( Romer, 2006 ; Kovash and Levitt, 2009 ) . That pitchers adapted to the ABS while batters did not suggests that which pattern prevails depends on how much an agent stands to gain from re-optimizing. Finally, we build on recent studies of the ABS itself. Lee et al. (2025) describe how the zone changed in the first half of 2024, and Lee and Ko (2026) show that count-dependent calls disappeared, a result we replicate. Song et al. (2026) attribute a decline in star batters’ performance after the ABS to the loss of umpire favoritism. We find evidence of this favoritism at the level of individual calls, but its value appears small, and much of the decline in outcomes appears to reflect the choice of a single pre-ABS season as the baseline. The rest of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 develops the conceptual framework and the hypotheses. Section 3 describes the institutional setting and the data, and Section 4 the empirical strategy. Section 5 presents the results and their robustness, and Section 6 concludes. 2 Conceptual Framework and Hypotheses 2.1 Setup Consider a pitch that the batter does not swing at, a taken pitch. It crosses the middle plane of home plate at location ℓ \ell (horizontal position and height), is thrown to a batter of registered height h h , and arrives in a context θ \theta . The context comprises the count, the batter’s reputation, the catcher, and the home-plate umpire. The evaluator calls a strike with probability S ⁡ ( ℓ , h , θ ) S(\ell,h,\theta) . Under a human umpire, S H ​ ( ℓ , h , θ ) S^{H}(\ell,h,\theta) is a smooth function of location. It may also depend on the context, through count adjustments, deference to reputation, or the catcher’s receiving skill, and it need not scale with the batter’s height. Under the ABS, the call is the indicator S M ( ℓ , h ) = 𝟏 { ℓ ∈ Z ( h ) } . S^{M}(\ell,h)=\mathbf{1}\{\ell\in Z(h)\}. (1) Here Z ⁡ ( h ) Z(h) is the zone defined by the league’s rules ( Korea Baseball Organization, 2026 ) . Its vertical bounds are fixed fractions of registered height, and its width is the plate (43.18 cm) plus 2 cm on each side; Section 3 gives the details. By construction, ∂ S M / ∂ θ = 0 \partial S^{M}/\partial\theta=0 . The switch from S H S^{H} to S M S^{M} in 2024 is the shock we study. Let v s ​ ( θ ) v_{s}(\theta) and v b ​ ( θ ) v_{b}(\theta) be the batter’s expected plate-appearance value after a called strike and after a called ball in count θ \theta , and let Δ ​ v ​ ( θ ) = v b ​ ( θ ) − v s ​ ( θ ) > 0 \Delta v(\theta)=v_{b}(\theta)-v_{s}(\theta)>0 . We estimate v v from 2022–2023 plate appearances, measuring the value of a plate appearance by weighted on-base average (wOBA), which weights each outcome (walk, single, home run and so on) by its average contribution to run scoring and gives outs a weight of zero. We call the weight of a plate appearance’s final outcome its plate-appearance value ; a player’s wOBA is the average of these values. On average, one strike is worth 0.135 runs. 2.2 Two components of the shock Let S ¯ H ​ ( ℓ , h ) \bar{S}^{H}(\ell,h) be the human call probability averaged over contexts. The change in the call probability for a given pitch decomposes into S M ​ ( ℓ , h ) − S H ​ ( ℓ , h , θ ) = [ S M ​ ( ℓ , h ) − S ¯ H ​ ( ℓ , h ) ] ⏟ geometric − [ S H ​ ( ℓ , h , θ ) − S ¯ H ​ ( ℓ , h ) ] ⏟ discretionary . S^{M}(\ell,h)-S^{H}(\ell,h,\theta)=\underbrace{\big[S^{M}(\ell,h)-\bar{S}^{H}(\ell,h)\big]}_{\text{geometric}}-\underbrace{\big[S^{H}(\ell,h,\theta)-\bar{S}^{H}(\ell,h)\big]}_{\text{discretionary}}. (2) The geometric component reflects the difference between the rule’s zone and the human zone. It varies only with location, height and handedness, and it is a redistribution chosen by the rule’s designers. The discretionary component is the part of human judgment that responds to context, and the machine sets it to zero. It is a set of rents created by the human evaluator: deference to stars, adjustments to the count, and the value of a catcher’s ability to influence calls. 2.3 Hypotheses Our first hypothesis, H1, is that the machine removes discretion. Holding location fixed, called-strike probabilities under the ABS do not depend on the count, the batter’s reputation or the catcher. The pre-ABS size of each context effect measures a rent that the machine removes. Catcher framing is a skill whose value comes from the evaluator’s errors, so it should be a persistent catcher attribute before the ABS and indistinguishable from noise after it. The second hypothesis, H2, is that the geometric incidence of the change follows the rule’s design. Because Z ⁡ ( h ) Z(h) scales with registered height and is symmetric across handedness, the ABS shifts strikes toward tall batters at the top of the zone. It also removes any handedness asymmetry in the human zone. The third hypothesis, H3, is that the economic incidence of the change equals exposure times price. To first order, the change in a batter’s expected plate-appearance value is Δ V ≈ − ∑ taken pitches Δ S ( ℓ , h , θ ) Δ v ( θ ) = − E × Δ ​ v ¯ , \Delta V\;\approx\;-\sum_{\text{taken pitches}}\Delta S(\ell,h,\theta)\,\Delta v(\theta)\;=\;-E\times\overline{\Delta v}, (3) where E E is the number of calls per plate appearance that the shock flips. Large changes in call probabilities therefore translate into small changes in outcomes when the affected pitches are rare. Where we observe an outcome change for a group, the call channel in ( 3 ) bounds the part of that change attributable to the ABS. The fourth hypothesis, H4, concerns pitchers, who should reallocate their pitches toward locations whose value rose, with partial adjustment. We divide the plate into five vertical bands (the three thirds of the ABS zone and the areas above and below it) and five horizontal bands (the three thirds of its width and the areas beyond each side). A cell c c is a pitch type (fastball, slider, curveball and so on) in one of the 25 resulting areas, and s t ​ ( c ) s_{t}(c) is the share of that pitch type’s pitches thrown to the area in season t t . The ABS changes the value of cell c c by its mechanical shock G ⁡ ( c ) G(c) , the change in the cell’s value to the pitcher, in wOBA points per 1,000 pitches, when its 2022–2023 called pitches are re-judged by the ABS rule with behavior held fixed. We model usage as partial adjustment toward a target, the reduced form implied by convex adjustment costs ( Lucas, 1967 ; Gould, 1968 ) : Δ ​ s t ​ ( c ) = λ ⁡ [ s t ∗ ​ ( c ) − s t − 1 ​ ( c ) ] , s 2024 ∗ ​ ( c ) − s 2023 ∗ ​ ( c ) = κ ​ G ​ ( c ) . \Delta s_{t}(c)=\lambda\,\big[s^{*}_{t}(c)-s_{t-1}(c)\big],\qquad s^{*}_{2024}(c)-s^{*}_{2023}(c)=\kappa\,G(c). (4) Three implications follow. First, the 2024 change in usage responds to G G over and above any pre-existing trend: if β t \beta_{t} denotes the slope of the usage change on G G in season t t , the acceleration A = β 2024 − β 2023 A=\beta_{2024}-\beta_{2023} is positive. Second, the response fades once the new target is reached, so β 2025 \beta_{2025} and β 2026 \beta_{2026} are close to zero; a small negative value would indicate overshooting followed by correction. Third, groups that were already moving toward the new target before 2024 show little acceleration, whereas groups that had not moved catch up. These implications require only that usage move in proportion to its distance from the target, not that it move slowly; they hold for any adjustment speed λ \lambda , including one close to one. The fifth hypothesis, H5, is that agents re-optimize only when the gain exceeds the cost. Even professionals can leave sizable gains unexploited ( Romer, 2006 ) , which suggests that changing a strategy is costly. Suppose that changing a decision rule carries a fixed cognitive or practice cost in addition to the convex cost above, as in models that combine the two ( Cooper and Haltiwanger, 2006 ) . An agent then adjusts only when the expected gain exceeds the fixed cost, so that adjustment is lumpy ( Caballero and Engel, 1999 ) , and the convex cost governs how quickly an agent that does adjust approaches its target. The two sides of the plate face different gains. A pitcher’s location plan is set in advance and applies to every batter, so its gain scales with the league-wide movement of the zone. A batter’s swing decision is made in a fraction of a second, and its gain scales with the batter’s own exposure E E , which H3 implies is small. We therefore expect pitchers to adapt and batters not to, even after the count stops affecting calls. 3 Institutional Setting and Data 3.1 The ABS in the KBO Since the start of the 2024 season the KBO has used the ABS in every regular-season game. A tracking system measures every pitch, and a strike-determination system relays the call to the umpire through an earpiece. Calls cannot be challenged. The rule defines the zone relative to each batter’s registered height. In 2024 the bottom and top of the zone were 27.64% and 56.35% of height. From 2025 both bounds moved down by 0.6 percentage points, to 27.04% and 55.75%, and they were unchanged in 2026. Horizontally, the zone is the plate widened by 2 cm on each side, 47.18 cm in total. According to the league’s rules, the horizontal bounds are checked at the middle plane of the plate, and a strike requires the pitch to meet the vertical bounds at both the middle plane and the back plane ( Korea Baseball Organization, 2026 ) . The published rules do not say whether a pitch that only partly overlaps the zone is a strike. Three other rule changes overlap with our sample. In 2024 the league limited defensive shifts (moving infielders toward the side of the field to which a batter tends to hit) and enlarged the bases; a pitch clock (a time limit between pitches) was piloted in the same year, adopted in 2025 and relaxed in 2026; and in 2022, two years before the ABS, the league instructed umpires to call a wider zone. None of these changes enters the call function S S , so tests based on calls are unaffected by them. Tests based on behavior and outcomes rely on contrasts within the league, by height, handedness, exposure and pitching arm, so that league-wide shocks are absorbed by season fixed effects. 3.2 Pitch-level data We collect every regular-season pitch from 2021 to 2026 from the play-by-play feed of Naver Sports, the sports service of the Korean web portal Naver, which publishes the league’s tracking data ( Naver Sports, 2026 ) . For each pitch we observe the call or batted-ball outcome, the pitch type and velocity, and the nine parameters of the fitted trajectory. We also observe the batter’s registered height and batting side (left or right), the pitcher’s throwing arm, and the result of the plate appearance. We add the four umpires listed for each game and the catcher on the field for each pitch, which we reconstruct from the starting lineup and the substitution log. We restrict the sample to April–September, so that each season covers the same months, and drop the All-Star Game. The final sample contains 1,203,755 pitches, of which 657,201 were called, and 308,959 plate appearances. Table 1 summarizes them by season. Among other statistics, it reports the share of high pitches, those in the upper third of the ABS zone or above (the top two of the five vertical bands defined in Section 2 ). The seasons play different roles. The two seasons 2022–2023 form the human-umpire baseline, and every quantity defined relative to the human zone is estimated on them alone. The most important is the human zone itself, S ¯ H ​ ( x , z ) \bar{S}^{H}(x,z) , the probability of a called strike at horizontal position x x and height above the ground z z . We estimate it from 2022–2023 calls with a logit model in which this probability is a smooth function of x x and z z (a generalized additive model with a tensor-product spline). Because z z is measured in absolute terms, the estimated zone is free to ignore the batter’s height. Two measurement issues require attention. The first is a change in the source format: from games on 16 July 2026 the source data report trajectories relative to a reference point 55 ft from the plate instead of 50 ft. Ignoring this would inflate plate-crossing heights by 12–19 cm. After the correction, the replication rate is identical before and after the switch (Appendix Table A3 ). The second is the stability of the tracking calibration, since a recalibration of the vertical axis could masquerade as pitchers throwing higher. Within a pitcher and pitch type, the height of the ball 50 ft from the plate, close to the release point (where the ball leaves the pitcher’s hand), changes by at most 1.8 cm across seasons (Appendix Table A2 ).
